# Volume 3 — Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Upon the arrival of the Christmas holidays, the girls belonging to Tabby’s Place departed for their own homes, yet Aunt Euphemia chose to remain right there.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0000 }

“I am unable to visit any of those locations where I received invitations while bringing along those three cats,” she stated. “Furthermore, I refuse to abandon the poor animals in this house by themselves for almost three weeks. I might do so if we were blessed with respectable neighbors who could give them food, yet this street contains only millionaires. Therefore, I will remain in this house and ensure Tabby’s Place stays warm until your return.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0001 }

Nell returned to her house anticipating her customary joy—expectations that were only partially realized. Upon her arrival, Brierley was locked in an unseasonably early, freezing, and tempestuous winter that surpassed the memories of even the “oldest inhabitant”. Massive snowdrifts practically encircled Grey Shutters. Ferocious storms raged on nearly every single day of that unfortunate break, and continuous drifting persisted even when the weather cleared. Whenever the roads were cleared, they promptly became blocked once more. Venturing outside proved nearly impossible. On three separate nights, the B.V.I.S. attempted to throw a gathering to celebrate the college students, but the gale proved so fierce on every occasion that no one could attend, leading them to abandon the effort in utter frustration. Although Nell cherished and remained devoted to Grey Shutters, she was unable to prevent her thoughts from drifting wistfully toward Tabby’s Place, with its comforting hearth, Aunt Euphemia’s laughing eyes, the trio of cats, the lively banter among the girls, and the delightful Friday nights spent with visiting college friends conversing about serious and lighthearted matters.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0002 }

Nell experienced loneliness; throughout the entirety of the break, Isolde was confined to her house due to a severe bout of bronchitis. Travelling to Grey Shutters was impossible for her, and Nell was seldom able to reach Pear Hill, because snowdrifts blocked the former path through the Whispering Wood, while the lengthy route across the icy Lake of Glassy Waters proved nearly as difficult. Opal Pettigrew lay buried in the snow-covered cemetery; Odette Pullen had taken a job instructing at a school situated on western prairies. Hugh, indeed, remained loyal, slogging through the snow to Grey Shutters on any evening he could. Nevertheless, Hugh’s calls were no longer what they used to be. Nell nearly feared them. Looking up during a abrupt lull in conversation only to discover Hugh’s hazel eyes locked onto her, displaying a completely obvious look in their serious depths, was extremely unsettling; even more unsettling was discovering that she was glowing flushed and uneasy beneath his look, precisely as if—precisely as if—well, the experience caused great embarrassment. Nell longed to be returned to Tabby’s Place, a spot where another person was constantly present to soften the tension of an awkward moment. Whenever Hugh arrived at Grey Shutters, Thirza immediately retired to Mrs. Sowerby’s area and made sure the twins accompanied her. The meaning behind this action could not be misunderstood, leaving Nell in a state of powerless rage about it.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0003 }

Robin, nevertheless, was thoroughly delighted. He delighted in stepping outside during the morning hours and clearing the tracks to the henhouse and well with a shovel. He took great pleasure in the Christmas-season treats that Mrs. Sowerby and Thirza competed to bake for Nell, and he was engrossed in a fascinating story, contained in a school library volume, about an extraordinary protagonist who appeared to possess an uncanny knack for stumbling into predicaments from which he was typically rescued by a volcanic explosion or an earthquake, which blasted him safely clear of his difficulties, dropped him into wealth, and concluded the narrative with suitable éclat.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0004 }

“Nell, I am telling you that the tale is fantastic,” he exclaimed with delight. “Reading it pleases me far more than reading the Bible.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0005 }

“Would you?” Nell smiled.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0006 }

Robin cast a curious glance toward her.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0007 }

“Nell, you appear not the least bit startled. When I mentioned it to Mrs. Sowerby, she was tremendously shocked.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0008 }

“No, Robin, I am not shocked. A nine-year-old child preferring an adventure book over the Bible seems entirely understandable to me. However, once you grow up, it is my hope and belief that you will come to understand how incredible the Bible is.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0009 }

“Well, I believe certain sections of it are good,” admitted Robin. “Take that tale regarding Joseph—it is great. However, had I been Joseph, forgiving the brothers would not have been my choice. Absolutely not, Nell. Off with all their heads I would have gone. Mrs. Sowerby became terribly angry when I uttered that, closing the Bible and declaring she would not read me another bit of it if I spoke in that manner. Therefore, I remain silent now while she reads it on Sunday afternoons; I merely formulate thoughts and share them with Milty Gammon the following day at school. I related the tale concerning Elisha and the bears to Milty, and it frightened him so much that not once has he mocked Mr. Pettifer’s bald head since. Do any bears exist on St. Brendan’s Island, Nell? I wish to learn.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0010 }

“No longer,” Nell remarked, her mind elsewhere, while a dusting of snow was hurled by the gust against the glass. “Oh, my, is the storm ever going to end.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0011 }

“God knows,” Robin remarked blithely, getting ready to go back to his book.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0012 }

This time, Nell felt a wave of shock.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0013 }

“Robin!” she cried out in a tone of rebuke.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0014 }

“That is what Mrs. Sowerby says,” Robin objected. “Thirza asked, ‘Will Ludovic Speed and Theodora Dix ever get married?’ one evening last week, and Mrs. Sowerby replied, ‘“God knows”’—in precisely that manner.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0015 }

“Well, she ought not to have said it,” Nell stated, quickly choosing which horn of this dilemma she would impale herself on. “No one should take that name in vain or use it casually, Robin. You must never do it again.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0016 }

“If I utter it slowly and solemnly, similar to the preacher, would it still not?” Robin asked with seriousness.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0017 }

“No, not even then.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0018 }

“Well, I shall not. Middle Welby is where Ludovic Speed and Theodora Dix reside, and according to Mrs. Agatha, he has courted her for a century. Will they not be getting too old for marriage soon, Nell? It is my hope that Hugh does not court you for such a length of time. Nell, at what time will you be getting married? Mrs. Sowerby states that it is certain.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0019 }

“Mrs. Sowerby is a—” Nell started with anger; then she paused. “Terrible old gossip,” finished Robin serenely. “Every person refers to her like that. But is it certain, Nell? I wish to know.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0020 }

“You’re a very silly little boy, Robin,” said Nell, walking out of the room with a haughty air. Nobody was in the kitchen, so she took a seat near the window while the cold winter twilight rapidly deepened. The sun was no longer up, and the wind had ceased. From behind a western ridge of purple clouds, a pale, cold moon peeked through. As the sky lost its color, the ribbon of yellow following the western horizon became sharper and more intense, giving the impression that every scattered ray of light was gathering in that single place; set against it, the far-off hills, bordered by priest-like firs, were sharply defined and dark. Nell gazed over the quiet, snow-covered fields, which appeared cold and dead beneath the unforgiving glow of that bleak sunset, and released a sigh. She felt extremely isolated and deeply sad, as she pondered whether she could go back to Wexcombe the following year. It appeared improbable. The sole scholarship available during the Sophomore year was quite minor. She refused to accept Thirza’s money, and there appeared to be scant chance of gathering sufficient earnings over the summer break.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0021 }

“I guess I will simply be forced to leave after this year,” she pondered gloomily, “and go back to teaching at a district school till my earnings cover the rest of my studies. By then, everyone in my former class will already be done with school, making Tabby’s Place an impossibility. Oh well! Cowardice is not for me. Having the ability to pay my own expenses if required is something I appreciate.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0022 }

“Mr. Pettifer is coming up the lane, wading through,” Robin called out as he ran outside. “My hope is that he has the mail with him. Three days have passed since our last delivery. What those pesky Grits are up to is something I want to see. Nell, I am a Conservative. And let me tell you, keeping your eye on those Grits is necessary.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0023 }

The mail was delivered by Mr. Pettifer, and Nell’s sad mood was quickly chased away by cheerful letters from Mabel, Honora, and Cressy. A letter had also arrived from Aunt Euphemia, who wrote that she was maintaining the home fires, and she noted that the cats were all in good health and the house plants were thriving.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0024 }

“The climate has been exceedingly freezing,” her letter stated, “which is why the felines were allowed by me to stay overnight inside—Smudge along with Joseph upon the living-room couch, while the Sarah-cat rested at my bed’s end. Hearing her purr offers true companionship whenever I awaken during the night and ponder my unfortunate child over in the foreign field. Were her location any place other than India, anxiety would not plague me, yet the serpents in that region are reported to be dreadful. Driving the idea of those serpents from my mind requires the entirety of the Sarah-cat’s purring. My faith suffices for all matters except for the serpents. Why Providence created them escapes my comprehension. At times I doubt that He was their creator. My inclination is to think that the Old Harry played a role in fashioning them.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0025 }

Nell had set aside a slender, typed note for the end, believing it to be of little consequence. After reading its contents, she remained motionless, tears welling in her eyes.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0026 }

“What is the problem, Nell?” Thirza inquired.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0027 }

“Miss Lavinia Pembroke has passed away,” Nell stated, speaking softly.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0028 }

“At length, she passed away,” Thirza remarked. “Indeed, she was ill for more than a year, and her death has been anticipated by the Pembrokes at any moment. Her passing brings a merciful end to her dreadful suffering, Nell. Toward you, she was ever gentle.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0029 }

“Thirza, she remained good to me until the end. Her attorney sent this letter. In her testament, she bequeathed me one thousand dollars.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0030 }

“My goodness, isn't that a tremendous amount of cash,” cried Robin. “Isn't she the female you and Isolde landed upon when the pair of you leapt onto the bed in the spare room? Isolde related that tale to me. Did she bequeath you such a large sum for that reason?”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0031 }

“Be quiet, Robin,” Nell murmured softly. Her heart overflowing, she stole off to the gable of the porch, permitting Thirza and Mrs. Sowerby to discuss the intelligence as much as they wished.
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0032 }

“Do you think Nell will ever wed now?” Robin wondered with concern. “When Dorcas Mott got married this past summer she remarked that if she’d possessed sufficient money to support herself she’d never have bothered with a man, though even a widower with eight children beat living with a sister-in-law.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0033 }

“Robin Farrow, keep quiet,” Mrs. Agatha stated with severity. “For a young child, your manner of speaking is simply shocking, it really is.”
{: #nw-v03-c18-p0034 }
